analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes and home-care providers from forcing residents into pre-dispute arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 13 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar skilled nursing facilities, Medicaid nursing facilities, home- and community-based services providers, and home health agencies that serve Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries from requiring or enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements — the contracts people sign before any dispute arises that force them into private arbitration instead of court. It would also nullify arbitration agreements already signed, and it puts any argument about whether the ban applies before a judge rather than an arbitrator. It never advanced past its initial referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future residents of Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes, people receiving home- and community-based services, home health patients, and their families. If a facility neglects or injures a resident, the family could sue in open court before a judge and jury, instead of being funneled into a private arbitration process chosen by the facility before the harm occurred. Existing arbitration agreements would become unenforceable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home and home-care residents and families

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits skilled nursing facilities and nursing facilities from requiring, soliciting, accepting, or trying to enforce pre-dispute arbitration agreements with any resident, whenever the agreement was signed.
Extends the same ban to providers of home- and community-based services and home health care under Medicaid, including their employees, agents, and affiliates.

Nullifies existing arbitration agreements: a pre-dispute arbitration agreement would not be valid or enforceable against a current or former resident regardless of whether it was signed before or after the bill's enactment.
Requires that any dispute over whether and how the ban applies be decided by a court under federal law, rather than by an arbitrator chosen under the contract.

Applies to the roughly 1.6 million people living in Medicare- and Medicaid-certified nursing homes plus home-care recipients, a population that is elderly, disabled, and often unable to bargain over admission paperwork.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, home-care agencies, and their liability insurers, which lose a contract tool that keeps claims out of court and away from juries; disputes would move to litigation, which is typically slower and can produce larger awards. Arbitration firms would lose this stream of disputes. Some of those costs could be passed on through prices or insurance premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and arbitration firms

drawbacks.text: The ban is retroactive: it voids arbitration agreements that residents or their families already signed, overriding contracts entered into under prior law.

The ban reaches far beyond nursing homes — it covers home- and community-based services and home health providers and any employee, agent, related entity, or affiliate — which could substantially raise litigation exposure across the long-term care sector and potentially push up insurance costs.

By eliminating arbitration, the bill takes away an option that can resolve some disputes faster and more cheaply than court, and the industry would argue the added liability could raise the cost of care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: residents who were harmed get their day in court, while facility operators and insurers bear higher and less predictable liability costs. The strongest good-faith objection is retroactivity — voiding contracts already signed reaches back to past agreements — and the breadth of the coverage of home-care providers and their affiliates. But pre-dispute arbitration agreements are usually presented as admission paperwork residents must sign to get care, so the main effect of the bill is to restore access to the courts for a vulnerable population at real cost to the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, referred to a Health subcommittee twice, and never got a hearing or vote before the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on January 29, 2024, with 10 original cosponsors; it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

On February 2, 2024, the bill was referred to the Health subcommittee; it was referred to the Health subcommittee again on December 17, 2024, roughly ten months later, without any hearing or markup in between.
The cosponsor list grew to 13, all Democrats, but neither committee ever scheduled the bill for consideration, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators, home-care agencies, and arbitration firms are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to use pre-dispute arbitration agreements that keep claims by residents out of court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators and arbitration firms

for.name: Rep. Linda Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 10 original cosponsors from House Democratic ranks.

for.name: 13 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Schakowsky, Bonamici, Chu, DeGette, Doggett, Frost, Nadler, Norton, Pascrell, and Tonko
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all 13 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral (both Republican in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; it sat in committee from its January 2024 referral through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Nursing home and long-term care industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of bans on nursing home arbitration agreements, which they defend as a voluntary, lower-cost way to resolve disputes.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on; the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care operators
industries.note: The bill bars these facilities from requiring or enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements and voids the ones already signed, exposing them to negligence and abuse lawsuits in court rather than private arbitration. Its interest in keeping arbitration lies in limiting jury exposure, which runs against residents' access to the courts.
Medicaid-funded home- and community-based services and home health providers, including their affiliates, would be covered by the same ban, ending their use of arbitration agreements with clients.
These firms earn fees from nursing home arbitration disputes; the bill eliminates that business channel and moves the disputes back to courts.
With arbitration agreements unenforceable, claims would go to juries, increasing the size and unpredictability of payouts the industry prices against.
Restored access to court for residents and their families creates cases these attorneys can bring; their interest here runs alongside residents' access to justice.
